#5032. ‘The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens’: Zcash team urges faster deprecation of legacy shielded pool

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

About 400,000 ZEC remains in the Sapling pool, worth about $291 million at current prices.

Zcash Zcash (ZEC) infrastructure team Zakura urged the network to accelerate the deprecation of its legacy Sapling shielded pool, citing speculation of mathematical breakthroughs at AI labs.

In a post early Thursday, Zakura recommended users migrate any ZEC still in Sapling to Ironwood. These shielded pools allow users to hold and transfer ZEC without publicly revealing transaction amounts or sender and recipient addresses.

"The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens," the team wrote.

While practical breaking of the pairing-based cryptography used by Sapling remains highly speculative, Zakura also recommended a network upgrade to disable payments into Sapling. Roughly 400,000 ZEC, or approximately 2% of supply, remains in the pool, according to Zakura, worth roughly $291 million at current prices. Zakura said most wallets support both Sapling and Ironwood, and the impact should be minimal, with miners accounting for much of the activity left in Sapling.

"Less than 2.6% of all transactions in the last 30 days use Sapling, and of those, 66% are known miner flows, and it's highly likely most of the remainder are miners as well," the team said.

An earlier Zcash forum proposal in April had suggested waiting a year after a community decision to make Sapling withdrawal-only. At the time, the proposal put its balance at 600,000 ZEC, down from 1.1 million at the start of 2024. Zakura did not suggest a new deadline in its Thursday post.

Zakura pointed to a reported proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and unsubstantiated rumors that AI labs had also made advances in integer factorization, the process of splitting large numbers into their prime factors. The difficulty of that task underpins RSA encryption, which is rarely used in cryptocurrencies, according to the team. Zakura said some math can be used for attacks on both RSA and pairing-based cryptography, so advances in one could help with the other, but the reported Riemann proof and the rumors do not show that either can be broken in practice.

"Practical pairing breaks are highly speculative," Zakura said, adding that transparent transactions and Ironwood do not rely on factoring or pairings.

Nevertheless, a hypothetical break in Sapling's pairing-based proof system would allow forged proofs, Zakura said, putting the funds in the pool at risk. The same cryptography does not secure users' private keys or their cryptographic records of shielded funds, so the team said developers could replace the proof system without replacing those records. However, Zcash would have to freeze Sapling before an attack compromises its state and users could then later recover their funds using a new ECDLP-based or hash-based SNARK, Zakura said.

Separately, the Ethereum Foundation doubled its protocol security team, The Block previously reported, arguing that AI is a "more urgent risk" than quantum computing and recommending Keccak-256 over four competing candidates for Ethereum's planned shift to hash-based cryptography. Zakura said it is also working on a proposal to add hash-based, post-quantum signatures for Zcash transparent transactions using SPHINCS+ with 192-bit security.

#5031. Nvidia to Pay $290 Million to Settle Long-Running Crypto Mining Revenue Lawsuit

Nvidia to Pay $290 Million to Settle Long-Running Crypto Mining Revenue Lawsuit

Nvidia has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a shareholder lawsuit dating back to 2018, resolving long-running claims that the chipmaker misled investors about how much of its soaring gaming revenue was actually driven by cryptocurrency miners.

According to a court filing Tuesday, the proposed cash settlement would close a case rooted in the 2017-2018 crypto boom, when miners snapped up Nvidia’s GeForce GPUs to mint coins, with the sales booked as gaming revenue.

As Decrypt reported, shareholders alleged Nvidia downplayed its dependence on that volatile mining demand, leaving investors blindsided when the boom collapsed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In November 2018, the company cut its quarterly revenue forecast as mining demand evaporated, and its stock tumbled roughly 28% over the following two trading sessions.

The settlement covers investors who bought Nvidia stock between Aug. 10, 2017, and Nov. 15, 2018. An analysis commissioned by the plaintiffs estimated Nvidia had understated its crypto-related GPU sales by about $1.1 billion over that stretch.

The company has consistently denied wrongdoing, arguing it could not reliably quantify how much of its gaming revenue stemmed from mining, and it is not admitting liability as part of the deal.

The case has taken a winding, years-long path through the courts. A district court dismissed the suit in March 2021 for failure to adequately allege the executives knew they were misleading investors. A federal appeals court then partly revived it in 2023, keeping the claims alive against Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang while dismissing those against two other executives, including Colette Kress, the finance chief who briefly served as interim CEO during Huang’s recent ouster.

The dispute then reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which heard arguments before dismissing the appeal in December 2024 without ruling on the merits. The district court certified the class in March 2026, and the $290 million figure emerged from mediation led by former federal judge Layn Phillips, whose recommendation both sides accepted in September.

The sum is modest for a company whose market value has swelled into the trillions on the AI boom.

Plaintiffs’ damages expert pegged the maximum the class could have won at trial at about $2.06 billion, meaning the settlement represents roughly 14% of those potential damages, a figure the plaintiffs’ lawyers note compares favorably with typical securities-case recoveries.

Those attorneys said they plan to seek up to 21.4% of the fund, or about $62 million, in legal fees, which they stressed sits below the Ninth Circuit’s 25% benchmark.

The settlement still requires court approval. Under the plaintiffs’ proposed schedule, the court would first decide whether to grant preliminary approval and send notice to affected shareholders, with a final settlement hearing to follow about 130 days later.

Notably, the deal is unrelated to the separate, far more recent turmoil around Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang, whose brief ouster and reinstatement this month over a spy-tinged scandal rattled markets.

For Nvidia, the agreement finally draws a line under one of the last major legal hangovers from crypto’s last great mining frenzy.

"Indeed, the speed of the outflows has, if anything, been more intense than the outflows from early May to late June this year," they added.

Last week, the analysts said retail investors likely drove much of the recent crypto ETF outflows and may have sold to buy stock ETFs. They also said bitcoin's price drop had widened the gap between its market price and their estimated production cost of around $86,000, likely adding pressure on higher-cost miners to sell bitcoin from their reserves.

#5027. What Is the Best Type of Yogurt? We Narrowed It Down to the World’s 8 Healthiest.

EVERYBODY LOVE YOGURT. Okay, maybe not everyone, but there's a reason yogurt has been a dietary staple in dozens of countries for centuries. Yogurt doesn't spoil as fast as milk, yet still delivers milk's nutrients—protein, calcium, potassium, magnesium—without the same risk of, um, certain GI issues.

"Most of the world is lactose intolerant and has been for thousands and thousands of years," says Robert Hutkins, PhD, a professor of food microbiology at the University of Nebraska. "Humans figured out that even if they were lactose intolerant, they could still consume cultured milks because the culture helps degrade the lactose before it gets to the colon and gets fermented by gas-producing microbes."

Whether you need help digesting lactose or not, the latest research suggests that yogurt has wide-ranging benefits, from enhancing gut health to improving blood sugar control to maybe even reducing your risk of an early death.

From Europe to Asia to Africa, all yogurt starts with the same basic ingredients: milk and good bacteria. But no two types are exactly alike. Here's what to know before your next grocery run.

Traditional Greek yogurt is strained through a cheesecloth to remove excess fluid. Yogurt factories use centrifuges or special filters instead. What's left behind is a thick, smooth yogurt with a slightly acidic flavor and a concentrated source of nutrients, including about 18 grams of protein per 6-ounce container.

Some food makers add thickeners as a shortcut, so check the label for a simple ingredient list of milk, cream, and yogurt cultures. "The products with thickeners added have a different texture, a little bit more gumminess," says Molly Kimball, RD, CSSD, a dietitian based in Louisiana. Swap in Greek yogurt for sour cream or mayo, or stir it into guacamole—the lactic acid slows down the oxidation that turns avocados brown.

Technically considered a soft cheese, skyr is strained like Greek yogurt to produce something firm yet creamy. It's usually made with skim milk, yielding yogurt with slightly more protein than Greek yogurt: about 19 grams of protein per 6 ounces. Use skyr to make dips hearty enough to stand up to cut vegetables (or chips). Or stir it into bolognese to impart a velvety texture and an extra boost of protein.

This yogurt variety isn't strained, so it has a thinner texture and less protein than its Greek or Icelandic cousins: about 6 grams per 6 ounces. Traditional Bulgarian yogurt gets its signature sharp flavor from high concentrations of the aptly named Lactobacillus Bulgaricus bacteria, which produce lactic acid. Kimball recommends blending Bulgarian yogurt into smoothies to add a tanginess that counterbalances sweeter ingredients.

Most yogurts are fermented in large vats. As yogurt bacteria digest milk, they produce a wide variety of metabolites, including gel-like substances called exopolysaccharides. Then the yogurt is pumped into the smaller containers we snag at the grocery store.

With French-style yogurt, the milk and bacterial cultures are poured into cups earlier, before the microbes multiply. "That gives you a more custardy product because it hasn't gone through this pumping phase that disturbs the gel," says Hutkins. Inside a 6-ounce cup of French-style yogurt, you'll find about 5 grams of protein. To try it the French way, eat your yogurt for dessert, alone or paired with a little honey or jam.

This tangy, thin, pourable yogurt is fermented with kefir grains–gelatinous clusters that contain milk proteins and up to 50 bacterial and yeast species. During fermentation, these yeasts can leave behind traces of alcohol and carbon dioxide, or fizz. However, many mass-produced kefirs use standardized starter cultures instead to maintain consistent product quality and keep the alcohol concentration low enough to sell in grocery stores.

Kimball suggests drinking plain kefir, Russian or otherwise. It packs about 8 grams of protein per cup. If you can't handle the sour flavor, balance it with a teaspoon or less of maple syrup or a few drops of stevia or monk fruit. If you want a flavored variety, pick one with no more than 5 grams of added sugar.

Sweet and mildly acidic, dahi is the key ingredient in Indian staples like lassi–a yogurt drink often flavored with mango, spices, or rosewater–and raita, the sauce that cools your mouth when you order your vindaloo extra hot. Some dahi varieties contain Leuconostoc, bacteria that produce a metabolite called diacetyl that imparts a buttery flavor. Each six-ounce serving of dahi packs about 7 grams of protein.

Drinkable like kefir, laban is sour but smooth and contains about 5 grams of protein per six ounces. Strain it in a colander or cheesecloth to make labneh, a thick, soft, yogurt-like cheese traditionally smeared on sandwiches and stacked on mezze platters.

This drinkable yogurt is often thicker than fermented milk beverages. Its mix of cultures, which hail mostly from the Lactobacillusgenus, imparts a moderately acidic flavor with subtle buttery notes. Amasi packs about 6 grams of protein per six ounces. It's traditionally eaten with maize or sorghum porridge, especially at breakfast.

#5026. What Is Artex? The AI Hacking Tool Linked to the US Spy Agency Breach

What Is Artex? The AI Hacking Tool Linked to the US Spy Agency Breach

The AI tool reportedly used to breach a system shared by three U.S. intelligence agencies is already part of the arsenal of at least six hacking groups tracked by Microsoft, according to research published Wednesday.

Artex, a framework originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals find security flaws, was reportedly involved in an intrusion affecting the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

The compromised system analyzes information collected from publicly available sources, according to the Associated Press. The identity of the hackers and the AI model they used remain unconfirmed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In one analysis, Microsoft's threat intelligence team identified both financially motivated criminals and state-sponsored groups using the software, including Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Storm-0940, and Storm-3358. Microsoft did not attribute the spy agency breach to any of them.

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

The CIA intrusion, disclosed Tuesday, affected a shared intelligence analysis system that draws on sources such as social media, commercial satellite imagery, and data brokers. A source told Nextgov/FCW that the breach had been resolved and classified systems were unaffected. What information, if any, was stolen remains unclear, though such an intrusion could expose analysts' investigative priorities.

The NSA suffered a similar breach exposing unclassified information, according to the New York Times. Prior, the NSA's classified internal communications network was restored on November 20 after several days of disruption. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed the outage to software patching rather than a cyberattack. The Donald Trump administration has denied that the recent outages were part of a coordinated attack.

Separately, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, a database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide that contains criminal histories, records of missing persons, fugitives, and stolen property. Investigators have not publicly established the extent of the intrusion or whether records were stolen.

Artex is not an AI model like ChatGPT's GPT or Anthropic's Claude. It is an agentic harness, a piece of software that lets language models interact with other programs and perform tasks rather than simply generate text.

A developer known as Autumn-27 published the project on GitHub in July. Written in Go, it was designed for penetration testing, the practice of attempting to break into computer systems with the owner's permission to identify security weaknesses.

The framework divides work among specialized AI agents responsible for planning, carrying out assessments, and reporting their results, according to Google's threat intelligence team. A shared record of findings helps the agents retain context and coordinate their work over lengthy assignments.

The underlying AI is interchangeable. Microsoft says Artex can use commercial and open-weight models, which means the framework is not necessarily subject to the safety policies of any one AI company.

Microsoft says that under certain conditions Artex can obtain lasting access with elevated permissions in minutes, rather than requiring someone to oversee each stage of an operation.

Artex attracted international attention in October after attacks on South Korean financial institutions. A November 13 FBI advisory linked the campaign to the theft of personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people.

Autumn-27 removed the original repository in October following reports of criminal abuse. By early November, researchers had counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed Artex installations, according to the FBI, though that does not mean all were operated by criminals.

Removing an open-source repository does not erase the copies others have downloaded or the independent versions they have created. Microsoft says that this month Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of Artex and began selling access to a commercial offering called Artex Pro.

The problem is not unique to Artex. Security researchers have long released tools that criminals later repurposed, but AI reduces the amount of manual work involved in running them.

The FBI has tracked Artex-related activity across 10 industries since August, including government, defense, finance, and technology.

On November 13, Amazon researchers described campaigns believed to involve Artex, including attempts to steal AI service credentials and circumvent identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

The identity verification system rejected every synthetic video attempt documented by the agents. Amazon also cautioned that it could not independently verify all the outcomes the agents claimed to have achieved.

As Decrypt reported last year, Anthropic said suspected Chinese state-sponsored hackers had already used Claude to automate 80% to 90% of the tactical work in a cyberespionage campaign targeting roughly 30 organizations.

Smaller criminal groups now have access to software that handles some of the coordination previously left to experienced hackers. They still need vulnerable targets, and defenders can still stop them.

Britain's National Cyber Security Centre said Tuesday that it had seen a sharp increase in AI-assisted attacks since September, with criminals exploiting familiar problems such as poorly secured accounts and misconfigured software.

For organizations defending themselves, the immediate priority remains fixing those weaknesses, reducing the number of publicly exposed systems, and improving detection. Britain's cybersecurity agency says today's agentic frameworks are relatively noisy, giving defenders a chance to spot them, though future versions may be harder to detect.

#5024. Your Guide to Running on the Treadmill This Winter

Here’s why it feels harder to run indoors—and how to hack it to make it more enjoyable.

There’s almost no other cardio machine that brings up as many feelings as the treadmill. For the first few years of my running career, I’d do just about everything I could to avoid hopping on one, even if that meant running in freezing temps or heavy rain.

Then, last winter happened. There was more snow and ice on the ground in New York City than I had seen in a long time, but I had a half-marathon to train for. It left me no choice: I had to move my workouts to the treadmill unless I wanted to end up like that meme where the woman says snow is the perfect texture for running just to wipe out on live television a few seconds later.

But, as any treadmill hater knows, moving a run indoors isn’t as simple as it sounds. A lot changes on a tread—form, mental stimulation, pace—and it can totally mess with your head. Once you understand why, though, it’s a lot easier to work with the treadmill instead of against it; here’s how.

Because it is! For starters, your form changes. “Many people shorten their stride on the treadmill—me included,” says Amy Woods, a USAT-certified run coach and ISSA-certified strength and conditioning coach. “We also tend to run a little more upright.”

There’s a simple reason behind it. When you’re running outside, your legs have all the space they need for each stride, but on a treadmill, you’re contained to the length and width of the belt. Plus, most people tend to stick too close to the front of the tread, making their space even smaller, says Morgan Mowers, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and V.02-certified run coach.

Between a shortened stride and the fact that it’s a bit easier to propel yourself forward when you’ve got the help of the moving belt, you end up using different muscles on a treadmill compared to outdoors. “We see a decrease in activation of hamstrings and glutes, those bigger propellers that push you forward,” Mowers says. Instead, you’re seeing more activation in your hip flexors, quads, calves, and knees.

On paper, a lot of these differences should actually make treadmill running easier than running outside. Another example? A treadmill provides a consistent surface. Outside, terrain and incline can vary with each step, so you call on more stabilizing muscles in your ankles and calves, Mowers says. “With every step, there's a little bit of a change when you're running outside versus on a treadmill,” she says. “Even if you are changing up the incline, it's the same exact surface over and over again.” You also don’t have to deal with the same environmental challenges—like heat and wind resistance—that come with running outside. There’s even a famous 1996 study that claims runners should set their incline to 1 percent to accommodate for the difference.

Even with all these easier-sounding differences, running on a treadmill often feels anything but. For many people, myself included, slowing down on a treadmill is the norm. One possible reason: You may just not be used to it, Woods says. Running safely on a treadmill, especially at higher speeds, takes practice. “It's definitely a different feeling when you're running on a treadmill,” Woods says. “You have to be more aware of your foot placement, your arm swing, and where your eyes are looking.” Even if you’re not consciously aware of it, your proprioception (your ability to sense your body’s position in space) could be affected.

Plus, when you’re on the treadmill, you’re stuck at one pace unless you change it, Mowers points out. “That consistency that your body is feeling on a treadmill can make it feel harder, and also may result in you going at an overall slower pace,” she says. When you hop on a treadmill, you start yourself at a pace and settle in until you physically change it. Over the course of a mile outdoors, in comparison, you may start at an 11:00 pace, then speed up to a 10:45 pace for most of it, and end up cruising at a 10:30 pace—all without really noticing. Even though your effort feels the same, your outdoor mile ends up faster.

Then there’s the mental side of things. Outside, you’ve got much more stimulation, says Rachelle Reed, PhD, an exercise physiologist. Your surroundings can offer the perfect distraction, and the natural variations in scenery, incline, terrain, and pace can help keep your brain more engaged too. This can have an impact on your rate of perceived exertion (RPE), Reed says. In fact, a 2019 meta-analysis found that at faster speeds, runners rated their effort as harder on a treadmill compared to outdoors. Basically, it’s harder to go hard on the tread. And because running on a treadmill is technically easier than running outdoors because you have less variation, wind resistance, and environmental factors to navigate at any given moment, that higher RPE really speaks to the mental effects of being inside, Reed says.

The good news? All these differences between treadmill and outdoor running only really matter if you’re training for a race. That’s because come race day, you’ll want your muscles fully prepped to accommodate your outdoor stride, along with the ability to run across inconsistent terrain and in various elements, Mowers says. Meanwhile, if you’re just looking to do cardio, you can take your pick between the two.

If you are in fact training for a race, how should a treadmill fit into your training? In this case, going outside tends to be superior to staying in, our experts agree. Don’t move your run to the tread at just any sign of inconvenience—running in the rain, cold, and (reasonable) heat all make you a better runner, and you never know if those conditions will pop up on race day, so you’ll be glad to have the practice.

Still, there are definitely situations where it’s not a good idea to go outside. Mowers draws the line when it comes to safety: If the ground is icy, snowy, or slippery in any way, she’ll stay inside to avoid potential injury. If temps are dangerously hot, she’ll run on the treadmill. If there’s risk from serious weather, like thunder and lightning or flooding, she’ll also stay safe indoors. And, she’ll stick to her tread in the event of poor air quality (anything that’s an air quality index over 101).

It’s always worth considering personal safety, too. If your only window to run is late at night and you feel more comfortable staying indoors, do that.

How hot is too hot? This is going to vary down to the person and place. Anything above 85 degrees can be dangerous, Woods says, and you also need to factor in dew point, humidity, and the effort of your run. (Harder efforts are more risky than easier ones.) If temps are higher and you decide to run outdoors, make sure you bring plenty of hydration and fuel, go slower than normal, and pay attention to signs of overheating.

There’s also the convenience factor. You may need to do a run on the treadmill because it’s more accommodating to your schedule or childcare needs. That’s totally okay too. Ideally, the majority of your runs (we’re talking about 80 percent, and especially your long runs) will be outside, but if you’re someone who finds themselves needing to do the bulk of their running indoors, a run coach can help you make sure you’re prepped for race day. (Woods works with athletes who do the bulk of their training on treads—it’s possible!) The treadmill exists for a reason, and your training will not be affected by the occasional indoor run.

First and foremost, don’t be too hard on yourself about pace. “I always disconnect from pace on the treadmill,” Woods says. Instead, she focuses on her time and RPE. It’s really about thinking about the “spirit of the workout,” she says. For example, you can pay attention to what heart rate zone or effort level you’re supposed to get to and match that—even if that looks slower and feels harder indoors.

And, no, you don’t need to set your incline to 1 percent to compensate for bringing your workout indoors, our experts agree. The biggest reason? The study that established the idea was very small (it had just nine participants) and done only in men. That said, the incline buttons will become useful depending on the kind of run you have on deck for the day.

Finally, give yourself a good warm-up on the treadmill, Mowers says. “Just the act of getting on a treadmill is going to increase our heart rate a little bit because we're a hamster on a wheel; we're trying not to fall off of this thing, and we're so aware of the fact that we're running,” she says. You may need at least 10 to 15 minutes to settle in before getting started with the rest of your workout.

Here’s how to approach different kinds of runs indoors.

Nothing really has to change, Woods says. It may take you a little longer to run a 5K on your treadmill, but try to stick to the appropriate lower heart rate zones and RPE that you’d normally achieve on these kinds of runs outdoors.

You can play with incline if you’d like—but it’s not a requirement if this is a one-off run you’re doing inside. Running for one day on a completely flat surface won’t affect your training. One reason you may want to try changing the incline may simply be because it adds some variety and stimulation, Woods says. If you’re someone who struggles because the treadmill feels boring, try increasing the incline anywhere from 1 to 4 percent for anywhere from 30 seconds to a few minutes every so often.

Another hack: Every 10 minutes, increase your speed slightly. That should give you enough time to warm up a little each time and settle into the pace, so you shouldn’t see much of a jump in demand on your heart rate or effort.

This one gets a bit trickier, Woods says. Going at all-out speeds on a treadmill can be much tougher—and not feel super safe. This is a time when you’ll want to think about the spirit of the workout. If you have intervals where you’re supposed to get to max heart rate efforts, instead of turning up the speed super high, you can increase the incline in addition to adjusting the speed slightly, Woods says. That should still get you to your zone 4 or 5, all while allowing you to stay slower and feel more in control. This is much easier to accomplish in a tempo run (where you’re holding the pace for longer chunks of time) compared to intervals, so you could also swap an interval run for tempo too.

You also have the option to skip a speed workout, Woods says. Missing one session won’t have an impact on your training, and if you’d rather not do it on the treadmill, you also have the option to switch it with another run for the week.

Now, here’s a workout that translates pretty well to the treadmill: All you have to do is up your incline for the duration marked in your workout. Woods recommends sticking between 1 and 4 percent as a good rule of thumb, but you can always bump up to 5 to 8 as long as you can keep good run form.

Ideally, you can move your long run to another day when you can run outside. But, if not, go by time—not mileage. Woods doesn’t recommend running on a treadmill for longer than two hours unless you are very experienced on one because of how it affects your form.

You also have the option to break up your run and do 90 minutes in the morning and 90 minutes in the afternoon. “This will help with form deterioration which is more noticeable and can be more dangerous on a tread,” Woods says.

While you’re on your long run, you’ll also want to incorporate moments of incline running and even some pace variation—both for improving your running and also giving yourself a mental reset. Woods also loves to sprinkle in 15- to 30-second walking breaks every mile or so to reset her form and hydrate.

Then the world is really your oyster on the treadmill, but all the same ideas apply: Focus on time and effort, not pace. And, feel free to sprinkle in different inclines and speeds to work different heart rate zones and find moments of mental reset.

#5022. The 21 Best Adam Driver Movies, Ranked

LET’S QUICKLY CUT to the chase: Adam Driver is a good actor. That’s probably an understatement to say the least; if Martin Scorsese, of all people, refers to someone as “one of the finest, if not the finest actor of his generation,” well, then, yeah, they’re probably pretty good.

Some may still think of Driver, who this month teams up with director James Gray for one of his best roles ever in the crime drama Paper Tiger, as Adam Sackler, the overly emotional Brooklyn boyfriend of Lena Dunham in Girls (a role for which he was nominated for three Emmys). But while he was obviously stellar in his breakthrough role on HBO’s hit comedy, it’s clear that he’s come a significant way in the time since first coming through to the public consciousness.

Driver has emerged in recent years as someone who works almost exclusively with elite, top-notch directors, headlining projects from the likes of Scorsese and Michael Mann as well as Spike Lee and Ridley Scott (just to name a few). He frequently shows his comedy (or, maybe dramedy) chops working with Noah Baumbach.

He’s also, of course, earned his presence on the blockbuster scene: while opinions abound with regard to the Star Wars sequel trilogy, it’d be hard for anyone to deny the intensity with which Driver dominates the screen as the main villain of those films.

For someone whose film career has only been going for about a decade, Driver has a remarkable resume and, having been nominated for a pair of Oscars already, accomplished a huge amount. As he continues to add more and more exciting projects to his ledger—he’s recently joined the cast of Marvel’s new X-Men movie— we wanted to rank the very best roles Driver has had so far.

Here are the best films of Adam Driver, ranked.

In one of his first leading roles, Driver gave audiences a taste of the intense leading man he would eventually become as one half of a deeply troubled couple (with a newborn child) in Hungry Hearts.

One thing we haven’t gotten enough of—in the post-Girls era—is Driver showing off his full comedy chops. In What If, a rom-com where he stars alongside Daniel Radcliffe, Zoe Kazan, and Mackenzie Davis, he gets to have a whole lot of fun as a romantic co-lead (and yell about having sex and eating nachos).

White Noise marked Driver’s fifth collaboration with writer/director Noah Baumbach. And while the movie didn’t wind up getting the Oscar love that it may have aspired for, it still found Driver giving a committed and intense—if deeply strange—performance. Fans of Don DeLillo's book upon which the film is based probably enjoyed what he brought to the table here.

One of the hallmarks of Driver’s recent career is working with as many legendary directors as he can possibly fit into his schedule. That includes three movies with indie king Jim Jarmusch; Father Mother Sister Brother cast Driver as a key piece of a striking ensemble, and delivered one of his most naturalistic and honest recent performances.

Speaking of legendary directors, Driver took the lead in Megalopolis, the maximalist, long-in-the-works sci-fi epic from Francis Ford Coppola (of The Godfather and Apocalypse Now fame), as an urban planner or architect of some sort in a bizarre future world. The movie is kind of a massive disaster, but Driver, as always, brings his all (with some legendary line-readings included). It’s hard to say it’s good, but you certainly can’t look away—and it’s clearly an experience Driver wanted. An important touchstone for his career in any regard.

Megalopolis is not streaming anywhere or available on physical media. You are on your own with this one—if you find it, let me know.

In a movie full of larger-than-life, outrageous characters (and even more outrageous accents), Driver manages to somewhat keep House of Gucci on the rails. He plays Ridley Scott’s Maurizio Gucci, and while he, too, has an absurd accent, it somehow winds up being the most grounded and reasoned performance in the whole film. This movie is camp, but Driver winds up playing it pretty straight—which mostly works.

Driver’s first collaboration with Noah Baumbach came as Lev, a dude who comes in and out of the life of Greta Gerwig’s titular character as she flails her way through her 20s. This light and fun character feels almost like the opposite of Driver’s intense turn in another coming-of-age-in-NYC-story, Girls.

In The Report, Driver plays Daniel Jones, the real-life investigator who led the search into the CIA’s use of torture in the aftermath of 9/11. This gripping true story isn’t one of Driver’s flashiest performances, but it may be his most pertinent to the world we live in today.

Driver made his first—and so far only—appearance in a Coen Brothers film with an ever-so-brief couple of scenes as Al Cody in Inside Llewyn Davis. He makes himself known in those scenes, though, as a gimmicky country music cowboy whose sole job is to say things like “OUUUUTER….. SPAAACEEEEE” on songs intended to be cheap radio hits. Still, Driver gives this character a sense of humanity in offering the titular musician (Oscar Isaac) a place to stay. He’s out of the movie just about as quickly as he gets into it, but it’s the definition of a scene-stealing turn.

This movie is weird! Driver plays a problematic stand-up comedian named Henry McHenry (that’s right) who’s married to an opera singer (Marion Cotillard)... and then they have a daughter, who is… a wunderkind musician, and also a marionette puppet. Things go way off the rails from there in a way that we wouldn’t dare spoil, but trust us on this: it’s pretty easily the most bonkers movie on this list.

There’s not much to Paterson—a film about a bus driver who writes poetry—but it’s one of Driver’s most unique and subdued performances, quite the shift for a guy so well known for going big and intense.

To play a Jesuit monk in Silence, Martin Scorsese’s long-gestating (but little-seen) 2016 passion project, Driver went full Method, losing nearly 50 pounds in preparation to play the role (according to co-star Andrew Garfield during an interview on The Late Show). This reflects on Driver’s performance, where he’s as intense and dialed in as he’s ever been.

By teaming up with the legendary Michael Mann (Heat, Collateral, Miami Vice), Driver manages to check yet another iconic director off his list. In this slow burn, brooding drama, Driver plays Enzo Ferrari, a win-at-all-costs businessman and racing team leader who finds himself, in 1957, at a crossroads with regards to both his troubled business and complicated personal/family life. Driver gives a subdued performance that scorches through the screen as the viewer constantly wonders whether he’s pushed one part of his life too far; he gives an Italian accent once again, by the way, and it goes a lot better than it did in House of Gucci.

Driver totally pops in While We’re Young, his second collab with Noah Baumbach. Here, he plays an ambitious and opportunistic Bushwick hipster who, along with his wife (Amanda Seyfried) meets an older couple (Ben Stiller and Naomi Watts) and become their “cool” friends. This movie is a very funny commentary on friendship, careers, and being content with getting older—and Driver’s character (a wannabe documentarian who doesn’t seem to have any sort of moral or ethical code) is a huge highlight.

Rian Johnson brought Kylo Ren to the brink in Star Wars: The Last Jedi, giving Driver’s striking, and, at times, maniacal villain the chance to really set himself apart from others in the franchise. The movie dives into Kylo’s relationship with all sorts of characters, including Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill) and Rey (Daisy Ridley), leading to an epic film-ending interaction with the former—and tons of confused fans online wishing he would get together with the latter. The movie leaves Ren in a position where he could have potentially become the most evil and powerful villain the series has ever seen; unfortunately, The Rise of Skywalker squandered all of it.

Imagine Steven Soderbergh’s Logan Lucky as the blue-collar version of his Ocean’s trilogy. Driver plays a war veteran bartender (who lost his forearm during a tour of duty) who, along with his brother (Channing Tatum) stage a major heist at a NASCAR racetrack. Driver plays his character as slow, but not a complete idiot—because this movie is far too smart for such 2-D characterizations. An extremely fun movie with a stacked cast.

Teaming up with writer/director Spike Lee to play undercover detective Philip "Flip" Zimmerman in BlacKkKlansman earned Driver his first Oscar nomination, something that even at the time felt overdue—but was very, very deserved. This movie plays strongly on the relationship between Driver and John David Washington, and finds Driver playing, essentially, two characters: his noble detective, and the person he has to become while infiltrating the KKK.

There are a lot of actors out there who reach a certain level of fame and get a little skittish when it comes to playing characters who could even potentially be seen as unsavory. In The Last Duel, Driver gives an absolutely fearless performance as Jacques Le Gris, a 14th-century knight who’s not only unsavory, but absolutely vile. The charm that we’ve gotten so frequently from Driver works to perfection here, as a character who at first invites an air of indifference eventually becomes so disgusting that he’s without question the worse of two evils. The Last Duel spends the duration of its running time asking questions about the truth and how it evolves over time—and while the specifics may be uncertain, the movie makes no mistakes about how heinous this character is (and how perfectly despicable Driver plays him).

Marriage Story brought Driver his second (and most recent) Oscar nomination, and a tidal wave of online memes (you’ve almost certainly seen him punch that wall more times than you’ve actually seen the movie), but his fourth collaboration with Noah Baumbach is probably his most impressive dramatic performance to date. Telling the male side of a dissolved relationship (Scarlett Johansson plays his soon-to-be-ex-wife), Driver finds the perfect mix of charming, charismatic, and delusional in playing Charlie, the man at (one half of) the center of the story.

After 2022’s Armageddon Time, James Gray had another largely autobiographical story to tell in Paper Tiger, this time more in line with his origins as a teller of crime drama stories. While Paper Tiger once again features characters based on Gray’s parents (this time Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson, after they were played by Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway in Armageddon Time), it adds a new character named Uncle Gary to the mix, played by Driver. Gary is a brash, lovable former cop, an ambitious businessman who goes around town like he owns the place and brings fancy dinners (shout out Peter Luger!) into his family’s home as a special surprise when he’s got a deal to spring on his brother. Of course, these kinds of deals in movies are never as good as they seem, and everyone winds up in more trouble than they bargained for. Driver plays the character in a gray area, and his plethora of charisma make it one of his very best roles to date. When he’s on screen, you simply can’t look away.

An onchain trade requires both the tokenized asset itself and an onchain payment that clears it. Most of this year's progress has been focused on the asset. Last week bank money started to move onchain too.

Last Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said that central bank money needs to stay the foundation of tokenized markets, with stables and tokenized deposits built on top.

Singapore has made progress toward that end. MAS sold S$100M (about US$77M) of 4-week bills issued natively on its own ledger, paid in wholesale central bank digital currency. Demand was significant, with bids coming in at more than two times the amount offered, with MAS planning more issuance and wider use as collateral in 2027.

Commercial banks are seeing the value in tokenized deposits too. Ant International launched a pilot program with DBS and Franklin Templeton for a protocol that settles tokenized deposits directly against tokenized money market funds.

The assets on the other side are already onchain. Tokenized Treasury and money market funds hold $14.1B, up 55% this year, though down from a peak of about $16B in July. The drop since July stems mostly from BlackRock's BUIDL and Circle's USYC, with the rest of the market increasing to a record $10.5B. As bank and central bank money scale onchain, institutions will be able to buy tokenized assets 24/7 with regulated deposits instead of private stablecoins.

Anthropic listed on Nasdaq on Nov 19, and tokenized versions from several issuers were trading onchain the same day. Across the 4 tracked by RWA.xyz, holders doubled from 2,161 on Nov 19 to 4,335 by Nov 22. xStocks' ANTx holds $25M of the $30M in combined market value.

With one stock split across many tokens, we expect liquidity to concentrate around tokens that redeem into real shares. Alpaca provides exactly that service and has processed $10B in minting and redemption.

That makes sterling the third-largest currency in tokenized government debt outside the US dollar. Most of the increase came from Aviva Investors, which launched a fund on the XRP Ledger in October and seeded it with £50M of its own capital.

#5019. Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

For the second time in weeks, a major Bitcoin mining firm has warned that attackers are siphoning mining rewards by hijacking the internet connections between miners and their pools, a sign that a long-dormant weakness in mining’s plumbing is now being exploited at scale.

Mining software firm Braiins said Wednesday that an attacker struck more than a thousand mining sites in a single second on Nov. 20, rerouting their connections to an impostor pool.

It follows a similar incident just last week, when mining-services firm Luxor reported that hackers had redirected miner rewards, which it tied to AI-assisted attacks.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The two firms described somewhat different mechanisms, but the effect was the same: hashrate quietly diverted away from the miners who produced it.

In its security alert, Braiins stressed the attacker didn’t need to break into any miner or into Braiins Pool itself. Instead, they exploited a long-standing flaw in Stratum V1, the unencrypted, plain-text protocol that carries work between miners and pools and offers no way to verify that the server on the other end is the real pool.

By rerouting traffic, the attacker impersonated the pool, fed miners legitimate-looking jobs, and pocketed the resulting shares under their own account at a separate pool.

The scheme hinged on manipulating the Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP, the trust-based system that tells networks where to route internet traffic. The attacker announced a narrower, more specific block of addresses that included a pool’s Stratum endpoint, causing networks that failed to validate the route to funnel miners’ connections to the impostor.

Hijacked machines kept hashing at full power while their pool dashboards showed zero hashrate, making the theft nearly invisible on-site.

Braiins traced episodes starting in early November across Latin America, mostly Brazil and Argentina, before a larger Nov. 20 wave hit mostly European miners, diverting between 0.6 and 1.9 exahashes per second at a time. The firm characterized the short, escalating bursts as the attacker “testing the waters,” noting the diverted hashrate grew more than tenfold in two weeks.

The technique isn’t new. Braiins noted that Dell SecureWorks documented the same routing trick stealing roughly $83,000 in mining rewards back in 2014, and the firm has warned about “hashrate hijacking” since 2020 as a reason to adopt the encrypted Stratum V2 protocol.

For years, the industry treated it as rare enough to tolerate; now, two firms in a matter of weeks have flagged it hitting miners in the wild.

Braiins urged the whole industry to act, recommending miners move to Stratum V2 or Stratum V1 over TLS with certificate verification, strip out plain-text backup connections, and push network operators to validate routes. It also released a free proxy tool for miners that can’t upgrade.

Any miner still on plain Stratum V1, the firm said, “is a target, on any pool.”

#5018. The 8 Best Standing Desks for Walking Pads, Tested and Reviewed

From budget picks to tricked-out options for a better WFH space.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even issues with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

“Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” says Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.)

But proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” says Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

To find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

While everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

Martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

At over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that important feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

While some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

During testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she says, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

This electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she says. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

Her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

This walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

Not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is important because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you plan to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.)

At the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

It’s important to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

We should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

I consulted with Bach and Darmofal to help identify what to look for in standing desks for walking pads. From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces. Our testers included Cori Ritchey, Lindsay Geller, Taryn Colbert, and Deanna Martin, who evaluated the desks for build quality, ease of assembly, adjustability, size, and overall functionality. Testing periods ranged from one week to over a month, with editors using their desks while sitting, standing, or walking on an under-desk treadmill. We also considered how stable each setup felt, how easily it fit into a home office, and any drawbacks our testers encountered.

#5016. Can This Supplement Really Fight Inflammation? Here's What Doctors Say.

NAC promises it can improve your health and longevity. That might be a false alarm.

IS THERE ANYTHING NAC can’t do? Well, if you listen to the supplement industry, no, not really.

N-Acetylcysteine, or NAC, in its supplement form, has managed to accumulate a large number of alleged benefits in recent years. Depending on who you listen to, NAC supplements can allegedly boost your immune system, detoxify your body, improve cognitive function, increase energy levels, slow aging, increase fertility, reduce inflammation, prevent respiratory infections, and decrease oxidative stress.

That’s a whole lot of responsibility to place on one single supplement.

Add that to the fact that NAC is a proven medical treatment for a couple of specific diagnoses, and you have the perfect setup. Supplement companies can extrapolate evidence into claims that go way beyond current scientific evidence. That’s been a blessing and a curse for NAC manufacturers—and a legal headache that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) just made a major move to solve with the proposed creation of a new regulatory category just for NAC.

The legal maneuvering is complicated and, if finalized, would allow NAC to be considered a supplement but still a medical treatment which technically isn’t allowed—yet. Basically, there’s a lot to unpack here.

So what can NAC supplement do? And what even is NAC? Is it safe? Let’s break it all down.

NAC IS A sulfur-containing compound, a precursor of the amino acid L-cysteine. In medicinal or supplement form, NAC is converted directly into cysteine, which is then used to make and deliver glutathione, a powerful antioxidant that the body uses to scavenge free radicals and manage oxidative stress. (Yes, the body is a complex system.)

While NAC isn’t found in food, cysteine is readily available in animal proteins, legumes, dairy, nuts and seeds, and some vegetables. Compared to dietary cysteine, NAC supplements are a faster, more stable way of increasing glutathione levels.

NAC supplements are available in powders, capsules, liquids, and tablets. And while NAC has legitimate medical uses, it’s not officially FDA-approved as a supplement as of this second. Of course, this hasn’t stopped the supplement industry from selling it—or influencers from promoting it.

NAC has been in a weird legal gray area for years. Because it’s an actual medical treatment, it technically can’t be classified as a supplement, even though it’s often presented that way.

The FDA’s proposed rule would classify NAC as the first-ever “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition.” Basically, it will be allowed to span the categories of supplement and medication, which has never been done before. If finalized, this ruling would “provide for the lawful use of certain ingredients in dietary supplements that would otherwise be excluded from the dietary supplement definition,” per an FDA constituent update.

The proposed rule would allow products that contain NAC to be lawfully marketed as dietary supplements, as long as they’re not otherwise in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act). In theory, this may eventually apply to other supplement-ish ingredients; Right now, this is centered around NAC.

The proposed rule is open for public comment for 60 days. It’s not clear when the FDA when issue a final rule.

This won’t really impact the general public if it’s finalized. Instead, it clears up potential legal issues surrounding NAC. “This will more formally allow sales of NAC over the counter, without a prescription,” says Jamie Alan, PharmD, PhD, a professor of pharmacology and toxicology at Michigan State University in East Lansing.

While some members of the MAHA movement have pushed for this, Alan says it’s also a case of “well, why not.” She explains, “It is generally safe, and I agree with that assessment. It is also being sold as a supplement already so, why not?”

Alan stresses that this move doesn’t suddenly legitimize all NAC supplements or claims surrounding them. “If you are buying a supplement, you aren’t necessarily guaranteed that the bottle contains what it says it does,” she says. “There really isn’t evidence yet in my opinion that supplementing with NAC as a dietary supplement will be life-changing for the vast majority of people.”

NAC is the standard treatment for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose. High levels of acetaminophen deplete the liver of glutathione, which is required for the body’s detox pathways. If you’re curious about the geeky scientific mechanism: Quickly repleting glutathione by way of an intravenous NAC infusion helps clear the excess metabolites from the overdose and prevent liver damage.

NAC is also a mucolytic, meaning it can break down thick mucus in the respiratory system. (Yum.) While recent research found that NAC may help with with COPD and chronic bronchitis feel less worse, more investigation is needed to clearly establish effects and benefits.

WELL, NOT ALL that much. Other scientific trials have looked at NAC’s effects on conditions including mood and compulsive disorders, Alzheimer’s, Schizophrenia, and chronic pain. Overall, results have been mixed and largely unremarkable. For most of these conditions and disorders, larger-scale clinical trials are still needed.

So while it’s true that research does exist on NAC and wider health benefits, most of the new research trials examining NAC’s effects use doses that are far higher than what the average person would take, and in forms that are not available to the public.

This hasn’t stopped wellness influencers from broadcasting that NAC supplements can help heal whatever ails you.

Many of these influencers argue that because glutathione may reduce oxidative stress, NAC is amazing for longevity and anti-aging. It’s simple, they argue: Because oxidative stress is associated with aging, increasing glutathione with NAC supplements slows biological aging.

Except raising levels of glutathione in the body does not necessarily translate into a desired outcome. Science agrees: There is no long-term human evidence that showing that this suppresses oxidative stress to the level of having a clinically meaningful outcome. Taking NAC for “healthy aging” is more marketing than anything else at this point.

FOR MOST HEALTHY people, NAC supplements appear to be safe in doses between 600 milligrams (mg) to 1800mg per day. However, doses on the higher end of that range may have a higher risk of side effects such as gastrointestinal upset.

NAC is not recommended for people with clotting disorders. There are also some potential drug interactions between NAC and immunosuppressants, so it’s always a good idea to get a doctor or pharmacist to cross-reference any supplements with the medications you’re taking.

Again, remember that the supplement industry is largely unregulated. Always buy from reputable companies, and look for products that are third-party tested to ensure that what’s on the label is actually what’s in the bottle.

NAC has some legitimate—and even life-saving—medical uses, and research is constantly evolving. But what the supplements don’t have at this point, is compelling human evidence showing that NAC has any clinically meaningful effects in healthy people.

Abby Langer, RD is the owner of Abby Langer Nutrition, a Toronto-based nutrition consulting and communications company

#5014. The 1Password Breach Didn’t Touch Your Vault. The Phishing Emails Might

The 1Password Breach Didn’t Touch Your Vault. The Phishing Emails Might

Password manager 1Password has disclosed a security breach in which an attacker accessed some of its backend systems and copied customer account information, though the company says the vaults where users store their passwords and other secrets were never touched.

In a disclosure published Tuesday, the Toronto-based firm said it began investigating on Nov. 19 after detecting that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The intruder used that access to reach

1Password’s source code and push malicious code to backend services, which then downloaded administrative data on a subset of customers. At no point, the company said, were vault contents accessible to the attacker.

Here’s what was taken, according to 1Password: customer names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys (which are public by design), certain protocol parameters that can’t be used to access an account, and non-secret internal metadata.

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the company’s software build systems, which hold some infrastructure credentials. 1Password said it has rotated all credentials that may have been exposed.

Crucially for users, the breach did not expose the data that actually matters: your vaults, the items inside them, the keys that protect them, or your account recovery keys.

1Password’s design means it never stores your account password or Secret Key, so an attacker who gets into its servers still can’t decrypt your vault. The company stressed there’s nothing you need to change in your account, and its apps and browser extensions are working normally.

What users should do, for now, comes down to what is generally good advice at all times: watch out for phishing emails, because they’re surely coming.

Because names and email addresses were exposed, affected users are prime targets for scam emails impersonating 1Password, particularly fake account-recovery or invitation requests.

The company urged caution with any unexpected message mentioning 1Password, and reiterated that it will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key, which you should only ever enter in the official app or on the official site after opening it yourself.

One wrinkle involves emailed invitation and recovery links, which contain a token. 1Password said a small number of users in that state were notified directly; as a precaution, it lengthened the verification codes in those emails from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters to make guessing them impractical.

The incident echoes a run of breaches hitting companies that hold users’ most sensitive data, a pattern that has emerged this year as attackers increasingly target third-party systems and developer accounts rather than the encryption itself.
