#4902. Vitalik Buterin calls for verifiable chips as hardware wallet threats evolve

Buterin warned that future attacks could use lookalike chips with hidden malicious functions, making hardware tampering harder to detect.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin on Thursday called for enhanced verifiability in computer chips, citing evolving security threats in the hardware wallet sector.

Buterin said in a blog post that most commercial open-source chips do not disclose enough detail to verify their physical construction. Publishing what a chip is programmed to do is different from providing a blueprint against which inspectors can check the hardware itself.

“This concern is not just theoretical,” Buterin said, adding that the crypto industry has seen attacks that involve inserting spy implants into hardware wallets before they get sold to consumers.

Buterin warned that future attacks could be harder to detect, with malicious functions built into replacement chips that resemble legitimate ones.

“This, you cannot detect with the naked eye,” he wrote.

In October, Ledger said malicious implants in devices sold through reseller CryptoBilis captured recovery phrases and transmitted them over cellular networks. Ledger suspended reseller sales in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, tightened distribution rules and offered X-ray inspections after tampered devices surfaced beyond the region.

Trezor in November said it found similar implants in three devices sold through the same reseller. The company released a firmware update to stop the implants from capturing data and reduced its reseller network by about 80%.

Related: Ledger’s early implant warnings deserved more action, Karpelès says

Buterin warned that inspecting chips would remain a specialist task for professional auditors, journalists and civil society groups, even if hardware designs became fully open-source.

“In order for computation to be democratized, the hardware layer must be open for participation and tinkering too,” he wrote.

Still, Buterin said that given extreme commercial pressures that companies face, the industry cannot expect all hardware to become open source.

He said he hoped the industry would split into performance hardware and secure hardware. While secure hardware might be “10x less efficient or more,” it would still be sufficient for most everyday applications.

#4901. What's on the Ethereum Roadmap: Glamsterdam, Hegotá and Beyond

What's on the Ethereum Roadmap: Glamsterdam, Hegotá and Beyond

Like all blockchain projects, Ethereum is under active development, with upgrades designed to make it faster, cheaper, and easier to use.

Instead of a single "Ethereum 2.0" event, the network upgrades through coordinated changes called hard forks that introduce new features or modify how the protocol operates.

Since the Merge in September 2022, developers have focused on scaling, lowering transaction costs, improving wallets, and making it easier to run nodes and validators. The Ethereum community is also aiming for roughly two major upgrades per year when research and testing are ready.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Ethereum's scaling plan relies on layer-2 networks. These are separate blockchains built on top of Ethereum that process transactions off-chain and send results back to Ethereum for security and settlement.

Many layer-2 systems use rollups, which bundle multiple transactions together and post them to Ethereum as a single batch, allowing Ethereum to support more activity without the base chain processing every transaction.

As a result, much of Ethereum's development has focused on making it cheaper and easier for rollups to use the network. More recent upgrades have also aimed to scale Ethereum's base layer directly, by raising the amount of activity each block can hold.

In July 2022, Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin described the network's six roadmap phases as the Merge, the Surge, the Scourge, the Verge, the Purge, and the Splurge.

These phases are not single upgrades but broad goals, and several progress in parallel.

Ethereum's roadmap is implemented through a series of hard forks.

Glamsterdam is the upgrade after Fusaka, and its name combines "Amsterdam," the execution layer upgrade named after a previous Devconnect location, and "Gloas," the consensus layer upgrade named after a star. It focuses on scaling Ethereum's base layer, with two headline features:

Glamsterdam also raises the gas cost of creating new state, such as accounts and contracts, to target database growth of about 120 GiB a year, and reprices reading stored data, to keep hardware requirements manageable as capacity rises. Under one proposal, EIP-8037, creating a new account would cost about seven times as much gas as before.

Other scheduled changes would make a standard ETH transfer between existing accounts up to 71% cheaper, let developers deploy contracts to the same address across chains, make ETH transfers emit a log that apps can track, raise the maximum contract size from about 24KiB to 64KiB, and speed up validator exits and consolidations.

Node operators and stakers will need to update their clients to support the fork; ETH holders do not need to do anything.

Developers originally targeted the first half of 2026. Glamsterdam went live on the Sepolia testnet in October 2026, but a fork on the Hoodi testnet planned for October 26, 2026, was postponed after security firm ChainSecurity warned that the upgrade's gas changes could weaken safeguards in existing smart contracts.

In November 2026, developers rescheduled the Hoodi fork for December 15, 2026, and agreed to ship the gas changes unaltered. As of November 2026, no mainnet date had been set.

Hegotá is the upgrade planned to follow Glamsterdam. Its name combines "Bogotá," the execution layer upgrade named after a previous Devcon location, and "Heze," the consensus layer upgrade named after a star.

As of its October 2026 update, ethereum.org expected Hegotá on mainnet in the second quarter of 2027, with a fork on the Sepolia testnet to come first, though no dates had been confirmed. Two changes are scheduled for inclusion.

The headliner, Fork-choice Enforced Inclusion Lists (FOCIL, EIP-7805), aims to strengthen censorship resistance by having a committee of validators propose lists of transactions that block builders must include, so that no single party can keep a valid transaction out of a block. Frame Transactions (EIP-8141) would let each account set its own rules for what counts as a valid transaction, rather than relying on a single fixed signature scheme. That would bring features such as social recovery, spending limits, multiple approvals and gas sponsorship directly into the protocol, and let accounts adopt signature schemes designed to resist quantum computers.

Dozens of other proposals are being considered, but none are settled, and the rest of Hegotá's scope is still being decided. In November 2026, some developers argued that FOCIL should be dropped to free up resources for work to protect Ethereum against future quantum computers, with a decision on Hegotá's full scope expected in December 2026. Forkcast tracks the live status of each proposal.

Upgrade names and scopes can change during development as proposals are refined before each hard fork.

Ethereum's roadmap continues to evolve as research progresses and upgrades are tested on devnets and testnets before mainnet deployment.

This article was updated in November 2026, and will be amended as as new milestones are confirmed.

#4899. This Historic Home Is Built Around a Spectacular Light Well That Looks Like a Connect Four Game

Long ago, in Barcelona, the laundry of the middle-class residents of the Eixample neighborhood was washed in the wells on Calle Aiguafreda, one of the city’s most picturesque streets. Washerwomen and their families lived in narrow, two-story houses, and the women would go to the wells every day to hand-wash clothes. It is in this unique part of the city that you’ll find one of architect Raúl Sánchez’s latest projects.

The lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building. From here, you can see the living area, a corner of the kitchen island, the bottom of the blue light well, and the white-painted beams. Santina chairs from the 1970s are by Carlo Sant.

“It’s a modest little two-story home on a street that has since lost its original function as a place to wash clothes. We were asked to restore it for a couple and their child,” explains Sánchez. The house faces two streets: Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers. Since there’s a five-foot difference in the elevation of the two streets, Sánchez decided to add a landing at the higher entrance off Granollers, where one flight of stairs descends to a lower level, which opens onto Calle Aiguafreda, and the other ascends to the upper level of the small house, where the bedrooms and a bathroom are located.

In the living room, the floor is made of terra-cotta tiles that echo the traditional clay paving in the home’s garden. A rectangular skylight is offset by 45 degrees from the rest of the room and lacquered in a deep blue, which is complemented by a red reading corner with a Wassily armchair by Marcel Breuer (Knoll), and a yellow folding screen. Between two Amanta armchairs by Mario Bellini (Hay) there’s an Altar side table by Ewe Studio (Tacchini). In front of them is a C cork stool designed by Jasper Morrison (Vitra). Atollo lamp by Vico Magistretti (Oluce).

Sánchez added a new architectural element: a light well that extends from a skylight on the roof through the full height of the building, illuminating even the ground-floor spaces, some of which are partially below street level. Pierced by a series of circular openings, like a Connect 4 game, and coated in a glossy blue lacquer, the light shaft evokes an ancient well while also serving as a contemporary, poetic, and functional architectural element.

Halfway up the ground floor, the house has a second entrance from the street. Sánchez added a landing there with two flights of steps: one leading down to the living area, the other leading up to the bedrooms and the bathroom.

A light well topped with a skylight runs the full height of the building, illuminating the spaces all the way down to the ground floor. The 45-degree rotation relative to the rest of the structure defines the home’s circulation and breaks up any feeling of predictable regularity. Perforated with circular openings and coated in blue lacquer, it gives the home a spectacular architectural feature.

It also stands out as an organizing feature of the home, thanks to its 45-degree rotation relative to the floor plan. “This rotated geometry allows for the dynamic opening and closing of different perspectives and circulation paths, thereby avoiding a predictable corridor-like effect,” says Sánchez. “The circular openings also allow for views between rooms and across different levels.” Cut into all four sides of the light well, the circles allow natural light to enter from the skylight on the roof. As the sunlight moves across the walls of the light well throughout the day, the spectacular blue lacquer comes to life.

A large, custom-designed installation by Raúl Sánchez Architects runs from the kitchen to the living room, organizing and defining the spaces. Most of it matches the color of the walls, but it transitions from pale-yellow cabinets in the kitchen to lacquered wood in the living room. Ceramic pieces by Catalina Montaña (@hellobigmontana).

A stone countertop with subtle yellow veining plays off the chick-yellow fronts of the kitchen cabinets. The 9091 kettle is by Richard Sapper (Alessi). Skan pendant light (Vibia).

At the foot of the staircase leading to Calle Granollers, the mirrored door to the bathroom offers a unique perspective on the living area and the skylight.

The first floor, which is a compact 431 square feet, is designed as an open space with living and dining areas, a small office, and a kitchen. At its center is the deep-blue light well, a graphic element that punctuates the mostly neutral color scheme. A folding screen made of wood and rice paper is a special feature for one of the owners, who once lived in Japan; it can either connect or separate the office from the living area. A small powder room is positioned at a 45-degree angle so the door can’t be seen from the main living area. Near the Aiguafreda entrance, a kitchen island, also placed on a diagonal, is clad in mirrors, helping to create a sense of lightness and maintaining the open feeling and flow of the space.

A view of the living area from the small office. White and terra-cotta dominate, accented by splashes of color. In the foreground is a Kyoto table by Gianfranco Frattini (Poltrona Frau).

The house is rooted in the history of both its neighborhood and the specific alley where it is located, and the chosen materials engage in a dialogue with the past. On the first floor, terra-cotta tiles echo the traditional clay paving found in the home’s outdoor space. Colorful glazed tiles adorn the sinks and bathroom walls, with reddish-tone lacquers and paints recalling the clay soil long found in nearby orchards. The glossy blue color and circular perforations of the skylight elicit water droplets from a washing well.

The light filtering through the circular openings of the blue light well casts a glow on the vanity, which is partially clad in red ceramic tiles that cover the countertop and extend up to the ceiling.

The Dioscuri wall sconces (Artemide) blend right in with the play of colors and both the round and rectangular shapes in the hallway leading to the bathroom.

“The mirror-like surfaces of the doors and the kitchen island, with their slight distortions, evoke the reflections on the surface of the water,” says Sánchez. “Above all, the renovation has made it possible to preserve all the elements that give the home its character and history while also integrating contemporary, energy-efficient systems.”

The light well, painted entirely in blue, is at once architectural, functional, and playful.

The home’s green installations include an aerothermal system for air-conditioning, heating, and hot water; a new floor slab on the first floor to limit indoor humidity; enhanced thermal insulation in the roof; and improvements to the thermal and acoustic performance of the façades and shared walls. In addition, the skylight opens to take advantage of a thermal stack effect, expelling hot air in the summer while capturing heat in the winter–transforming the project’s central design element into a system that is both functional and contributes to the home’s environmental sustainability. The interior renovation is only the first phase of the project: Sánchez is currently redesigning the narrow garden, a plot that’s 13 feet wide by 98 feet long.

This home tour was first published by Architectural Digest Spain. It was translated by John Newton.

In the child‘s room, primary colors and a 1980s vibe dominate. The Veronica chair is by Afra and Tobia Scarpa (Casas). The AJ lamp is by Arne Jacobsen (Louis Poulsen).

A view into the light well, which provides illumination and ventilation.

A view of the hallway and staircase from the primary bedroom, whose entryway is painted red, setting the stage for the entrance into the room. Extra-large, veined-wood cabinet handles adorn the full-height cabinet fronts. In the foreground, a Reno chair by Federico Correa and Alfonso Milá from 1961. The Dioscuri wall sconce is by Artemide.

The primary bedroom, located under the roof, is bathed in light. The custom built-in storage units (Raúl Sánchez Architects) feature a stepped design, and the spectacular wood handles, with their prominent grain, add a circular geometric pattern to the space.

The house’s arbor gives it a rural charm, especially surprising given its location in the heart of Barcelona.

#4898. 7 bizarre things crypto whales spent a fortune on

The crypto rich have spent their fortunes on everything from dinosaur skeletons to rotting fruit, with some purchases defying belief.

They say a fool and his money are soon parted, but perhaps the idiom should be extended to crypto multi-millionaires and billionaires, who get their kicks from spending their fortunes on some truly bizarre things.

From a trip to space funded with Bitcoin to a $69 million nonfungible token, check out the seven weirdest ways crypto fortunes have been allocated so far.

For some early Bitcoin adopters, the ultimate luxury purchase wasn’t a Lambo or a Malibu mansion; it was a ticket off the planet.

In November 2013, British entrepreneur and Virgin Group founder Richard Branson announced that Virgin Galactic would accept BTC for spaceflight tickets.

At $250,000 a pop, the announcement piqued the interest of some of crypto’s earliest investors. In March 2014, Gemini co-founders Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss each purchased a ticket using Bitcoin to fund the space plunge — which they never actually took.

Bitcoin, space and beyond. Source: Winklevoss Capital

After stumping up 312.5 BTC each, the flights were repeatedly delayed until the Virgin Galactic VSS Unity was officially retired from spaceflight in June 2024.

Tron founder Justin Sun did make it into space briefly on Blue Origin in 2025 for $28 million, while f2pool co-founder Chun Wang actually commanded SpaceX’s Fram2 mission.

It was the first human spaceflight to fly over both poles of the earth. It’s not known how much he paid for the privilege but estimates suggest the four person mission would cost around $220 million.

Everyone’s heard of Bitcoin Pizza Day, when developer Laszlo Hanyecz infamously spent 10,000 BTC on two pizzas, but Bitcoin Banana Day gets considerably less attention.

Yet few examples capture the intersection of crypto and wealth quite like Justin Sun’s outrageous spend on, well, a banana.

Related: Pudgy Penguins expands retail footprint with Target trading card rollout

In November 2024, the founder of Tron paid $6.24 million for Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan’s Comedian, which consists of a banana duct-taped to a wall.

Sun subsequently followed through on a promise to eat the artwork, holding a press conference in Hong Kong where he took a bite out of the yellow fruit. If it were anyone else it might have been a Dada-esque artistic statement about the transience of worth in a consumption-based society, but it was Justin Sun, so it was probably just a publicity stunt.

He could have just gone to the 7-Eleven down the street and scored a banana for $1.50, but then he wouldn’t have been able to attract so much attention by eating it. The actual work he bought wasn’t the banana or duct tape, it was a certificate of authenticity for instructions on how to tape the banana to a wall.

Some people spend their fortunes trying to live more comfortably; others are more interested in the chance to live again.

Hal Finney, one of Bitcoin’s earliest contributors and the recipient of the first Bitcoin transaction from Satoshi Nakamoto, was cryopreserved after his death in August 2014.

Finney was a member of the Alcor Life Extension Foundation for more than two decades, and after his death, his body was preserved in the hopes that future medical technology might one day make revival possible.

Even better? Finney’s cryopreservation was paid for through a combination of life insurance and Bitcoin donated by fans. Crypto investor Peter Theil and “Bitcoin Jesus” Roger Ver are also set to undergo the process. Ver told Magazine back in 2021 he’d actually seriously considered killing himself and being cryptopreserved to be revived later, to avoid being sent to jail as a 23-year old.

Some collectors want paintings on their walls, others want bananas, and others still want something that has been dead for 69 million years.

In 2025, a group of investors, including Yoann Turpin, co-founder of cryptocurrency market maker Wintermute, spent $5 million on a dinosaur skeleton.

Yoann Turpin spent $5 million on a dinosaur skeleton. Source: Bloomberg

The Triceratops fossil is one of only two dozen or so known specimens, and was shipped from Wyoming to Turpin’s storage facility in Singapore.

Beyond the obvious novelty value, he reportedly said its appeal includes the fossil’s scarcity, which he likened to Bitcoin’s limited supply. One dino-skeleton will always equal one dino-skeleton.

From one enthusiastic collector of old relics to another. Patrick Gruhn, former head of FTX Europe, spent a chunk of his crypto fortune on a gold pocket watch recovered from the body of John Jacob Astor IV, the wealthiest passenger aboard the Titanic.

Related: 10 weirdest things ever tokenized... including farts

Gruhn spent $1.5 million at auction in 2024 and reportedly bought the old timepiece as a gift for his wife, partly because of his fascination with the Astor family’s history, and perhaps partly due to an affinity for sinking ships.

HEX founder Richard Heart’s taste in luxury goods could hardly be called understated.

In February 2022, he acquired The Enigma, a 555.55-carat black diamond, for approximately $4.3 million.

The enormous stone, also known as a carbonado diamond, is one of the largest faceted diamonds ever offered at auction, and the theories of its origins stretch from deep inside the Earth’s core to outer space.

Richard Heart bought a 555.55-carat black diamond. Source: Rapaport

Heart later renamed it the HEX.com diamond, connecting the unusual purchase to his cryptocurrency project. The US Securities and Exchange Commission launched a civil case in 2023 alleging that he misappropriated investor assets, including funds used to purchase the diamond. Heart was arrested in Turkey earlier this year due to an Interpol Red Notice connected to separate Finnish tax fraud charges.

What to buy for the person who has it all?

A $69 million NFT, perhaps. That’s what cryptocurrency investor MetaKovan paid in March 2021 for EVERYDAYS: THE FIRST 5000 DAYS, a digital collage by artist Beeple of 5,000 images created over 13 years.

At 42,329.453 Ether, the sale made it not only the most expensive NFT ever sold at the time, but also one of the most expensive artworks by a living artist.

The owner has no intention of selling the work, but it seems unlikely to fetch a similar price today. But he has purchased himself a notable place in art and crypto history.

#4897. Trying to Build Muscle and Lose Fat? Don’t Overlook This Part of Body Recomp

Crushing your workouts is only half the equation.

When it comes to body recomposition, showing up and crushing your workouts is only half the equation. You also need to pay attention to your nutrition to build muscle and lose fat.

And that part of the job isn’t always as straightforward as exercise. In the gym, you know you need to regularly lift enough to challenge your muscles and get your cardio in. In the kitchen, body recomposition typically involves two key things: getting enough protein and managing your calorie intake. As simple as that sounds, it isn’t always easy.

There are a few ways to approach these goals, but one key to making them more sustainable and manageable (and therefore easier to stick to!) is to track your macronutrients, or macros. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats, and protein, and each plays a unique role in your body recomposition journey.

Carbs get a lot of unnecessary hate, but they’re your body’s primary energy source, says Dana White, RD. Your body relies on glucose, a sugar that is broken down from carbs. Without enough of it, your energy, concentration, and mood can all be affected.

Fats are vital to your body’s overall functioning. They support the health of your cells, help your body absorb vitamins like A, D, E, and K, and play a big role in satiety, White says. Protein, perhaps the most obvious of the three, plays a major role in muscle repair and development—important at any time, but especially on a body recomp journey.

Counting your macros can help you stay on track with your body recomposition journey. To find out how much of each macro you need and how to fill your plate, try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide.

Cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

#4896. AI-Powered GTA 6 PC Ports Now Have Multiplayer as Modders Unlock 30 and 60 FPS

AI-Powered GTA 6 PC Ports Now Have Multiplayer as Modders Unlock 30 and 60 FPS

Gamers managed to get multiplayer working on GTA 6 for PC before Rockstar Games managed to release GTA 6 for PC. And they're apparently making the console version run better than the original, too.

A developer going by TeK shared footage Thursday showing multiple players interacting within the same game world in an unofficial PC build of Grand Theft Auto 6. The implementation reportedly supports character and vehicle synchronization, as well as proximity voice chat, running at between 25 and 30 frames per second (FPS).

GTA VI Working Multiplayer, Character, Vehicles & Proximity voice chat. (25-30FPS)#GTAVI #GTA6 pic.twitter.com/PyWvg764zZ

The development comes just a day after Decrypt reported that some AI-assisted ports were struggling to achieve 20 FPS while consuming upwards of 40 GB of system memory.

Another development team, known as BoYoo, demonstrated gameplay averaging 27 FPS during a boat mission, using an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D processor, an Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics card, and 32 GB of RAM. Memory consumption dropped to approximately 15.4 GB, although performance in the more demanding downtown areas of Vice City remains untested.

No son 60 FPS en el GTA de los Mares del SUR en PS5 pero NADA MAL CHAVALES!! pic.twitter.com/L63ALb7JAu

— NanospeedGamer (@NanospeedGamer) November 26, 2026

Developers have also demonstrated in-game modification menus, allowing them to manipulate elements of the game for debugging purposes.

Meanwhile, console modders have released a patch that removes GTA 6's 30 FPS cap on jailbroken PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles. The latter reportedly exceeds 50 FPS during gameplay without relying on AI-generated intermediate frames.

The patch doesn't guarantee a consistent 60 FPS, but it does offer the potential for smoother gameplay and more responsive controls than Rockstar's officially supported version. For some players, modifying their console could arguably provide a better gameplay experience.

The advancements come despite Rockstar's parent company, Take-Two Interactive, successfully taking down 3,007 GitHub repositories associated with Project Leonida, one of the most prominent efforts to bring the game to PC using AI coding tools.

Developers are using AI to reverse-engineer a leaked Xbox build of the game and adapt its code to run on computers, dramatically accelerating a process that traditionally required extensive manual work.

Rockstar has historically made PC gamers wait. Grand Theft Auto 5 arrived on PC in April 2015, roughly 19 months after its original console release, while Red Dead Redemption 2 took just over a year.

Generative AI could make that business strategy considerably riskier.

Obbe Vermeij, a former technical director at Rockstar North, warned about precisely this scenario before GTA 6's release.

“I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC,” Vermeij told Rock Paper Shotgun in an interview.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short NVDA with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Vermeij estimated that such an undertaking could cost tens of thousands of dollars in AI processing. Even if the resulting product fell short of Rockstar's official version, he suggested it could be good enough to satisfy some PC gamers, giving the company an incentive to bring its release dates closer together.

Wall Street has been paying attention, too.

During Take-Two's November 9 earnings call, Raymond James analyst Andrew Marok asked management how AI-assisted reverse engineering and decompilation were affecting the company's approach to security and development.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick acknowledged that piracy would become more challenging, although he maintained that replicating the intended experience of its games would remain technically difficult.

“I think it will be manageable, and we are focused on it,” Zelnick said.

There is some academic research suggesting that early piracy can substantially affect video game sales. A 2024 study published in Entertainment Computing by researcher William Volckmann examined games protected by Denuvo, an anti-piracy technology, and estimated average revenue losses of 20% when that protection was broken particularly early in a game's commercial life.

That figure cannot be directly extrapolated to GTA 6, which has yet to enter the PC market. But a sufficiently polished unofficial port distributed for free months before Rockstar's commercial release could reduce the number of players willing to pay full price for the same story they have already completed.

Rockstar would still have advantages, including official multiplayer servers, technical support, downloadable content, and a more polished gaming experience. The unofficial multiplayer implementation remains far removed from the scale of GTA Online, and none of the community projects has independently demonstrated that the entire campaign can be completed reliably.

GTA 6 generated an estimated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day alone, according to a regulatory filing by Take-Two. Twenty percent of that would amount to roughly $758 million in lost sales revenue.

Rockstar still hasn't announced a PC release date.

#4894. This Designer Finds Unexpected Beauty in Marble’s Leftovers

Wandering through the ruins of Pompeii, the ancient Roman city frozen in time by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, one is struck by that civilization’s devotion to precious materials. Surviving mosaics depict the opulence that once filled the city’s lavish homes. These fragments of classical life, and the richness with which they were rendered, captured the imagination of Polish-born designer Daniel Kolodziejczak, inspiring his upcoming Tesserae series for the New York design gallery Ateliers Courbet.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

Sun hits a pendant in rock crystal and smoky quartz.

Kolodziejczak creates objects in marble, precious stones, and bronze at his workshop in Carrara, Italy.

Kolodziejczak, who started as a jewelry designer in Paris for brands like Givenchy and Saint Laurent, began making decorative objects and furniture after a move to Milan. His exhibition at Ateliers Courbet (on view until January 16, 2027) was inspired by fragments of leftover stone he found in the marble yards of Carrara, not far from his workshop. “Every time I go there I find myself buying new stones,” Kolodziejczak says.

Kolodziejczak with two vessels from his Tesserae series

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

The designer polishes the base to a console from his Tesserae series.

The remnants accumulated in his studio until, on a visit to Pompeii, he had “the idea to bring them together” in one exhibition. His vessel shapes, inspired by antique Roman pottery, are hand-carved in marble, along with materials like rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz. The series will also include a monumental crystal pendant light, sconces in bronze with citrine quartz shades, a mirror, and massive stone tables. But despite the expansive scale, Kolodziejczak’s sensibility remains rooted in the concept of adornment. “I treat furniture like jewelry,” says the designer, whose Studio Daniel K is based in Milan and Paris. “These pieces aren’t meant to take up the entire room—just to be that accent of something extraordinary.”

#4893. Should We All Be Seeing a Concierge Doctor?

Paying an out-of-pocket fee could deliver faster, more accessible medical care. What’s the catch?

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

For as long as I can remember, going to my primary care doctor has been simple: I’d schedule an appointment a few weeks (or months) in advance, commute across town for an in-person appointment, and hope that my insurance covered whatever labs were ordered. But lately, many people have been opting for a membership-based system where they pay a monthly or annual fee for on-demand care. This concept is called concierge medicine.

Over the past few years, the number of concierge medicine services like Tia and One Medical has skyrocketed. Between 2018 and 2023, the number of direct primary care and concierge practice sites grew by roughly 83 percent, per a 2025 study in Health Affairs. (But there are also concierge practices specific to gynecology, longevity medicine, and even emergency medicine.)

“Over the course of my career, I've seen a lot of frustrations that patients have had in terms of access to care, long wait times, lack of continuity of care,” says Jane Zhu, MD, a primary care provider and associate professor of medicine at Oregon Health and Science University, and author of the Health Affairs study. There’s a real need for faster, more on-demand medical care—and concierge medicine is one way that patients are getting that.

Membership prices vary, with some costing as little as $9 a month for on-demand urgent and primary care, and others costing as much as $45,000 a year for top-tier care (at-home doctor visits for urgent care, X-ray imaging from your bed, and even private jets on standby for medical evacuation while you’re traveling). If you don’t live in a major city, many of these programs offer telehealth services all over the country.

So, what’s the catch? Ahead, read up on everything you need to know about concierge medicine, including the pros and cons, and who it’s right for.

The premise is simple: paying a membership fee unlocks extra attention and access to care from your doctor.

At most traditional clinics and hospitals, the goal is for doctors to see as many patients a day as possible. (More visits equals more insurance claims and/or copays, which in turn makes money for the practice.) With concierge medicine, doctors don’t operate within this same construct. Instead, they make money from membership fees, which means they can still turn a profit with a much smaller pool of patients. When you schedule an appointment with a concierge doctor, you’re not competing with hundreds of other patients for a time slot in the same way you would for a traditional doctor.

When Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai, worked in traditional medicine, she only got about 15 to 20 minutes for each patient visit. Now, she has the freedom to extend her visits to 45 to 60 minutes and form closer relationships with her patients. “I'm able to go into deeper discussions from a more holistic perspective and have a different type of conversation,” she says. Talking more in depth about sleep, nutrition, and lifestyle habits in general is key to helping her patients prevent illnesses in the first place—not just treat them when they come up.

Additionally, getting lab work done through concierge medicine may be a smoother process. While some traditional practices may have you drop by LabCorp to get your blood drawn, for example, many concierge practices will just do it on site, and even go beyond your average complete blood count for in-depth lipid, hormone, and genetic panels. But everything isn't always included in the membership, so check before they draw.

When you need a specialist outside of your concierge practice, they’ll often have health navigators—people whose job it is to schedule your appointments for you, facilitate communication between your providers, coordinate prescriptions, and run point on any insurance claims. Because the health care system can feel so fragmented and hard to understand, the health navigation piece is a major highlight for many patients, says Scott Braunstein, MD, an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care.

Regarding costs outside of the membership fee and bloodwork, every concierge practice is different. At Tia, for example, preventative care services like yearly physicals or vaccinations are usually covered by insurance, but diagnostic appointments often come with additional out-of-pocket fees. That means that if you come in for a UTI, sick visit, or complaint about a new health problem, it’ll often result in an additional charge on the patient’s end. The average copay for these kinds of visits at Tia is between $15 and $75—not too different from a traditional doctor’s appointment. However, at a high-end program where you pay entirely out of pocket, the care is pretty all-inclusive.

As of now, there isn’t enough data on concierge medicine to determine whether this model provides superior health outcomes for patients—like fewer hospitalizations or better chronic disease management—compared to traditional systems. That being said, there is one undeniable factor that contributes to good health: regularly going to the doctor. A 2026 report by the health policy initiative Milbank Memorial Fund found that people with chronic illnesses who regularly see a primary care provider have lower rates of hospitalization and emergency room visits—and lower health care costs on the whole.

However, in the U.S., about one-third of adults don’t have a usual source of primary care, per the report. Concierge medicine is one way to bridge this gap of primary care access, and give people an easy, on-demand way to take care of their health. Appointments are easier to schedule, can often be taken from your phone or computer, and the experience is designed to just be more enjoyable and convenient. “When we remove barriers for people accessing care, people are more likely to engage in their health. And when people are more likely to engage in their health, they have better health outcomes,” says Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the vice president of In-Office Care at One Medical.

If you can get into these models of care, they seem to be beneficial for both the clinician and the patient. But the question remains: “What happens if you can't get into those models of care?” says Dr. Zhu.

The number of clinicians practicing in membership-based clinics grew by 78 percent between 2018 and 2023, per the Health Affairs study. That means that more clinicians are leaving traditional medicine for this model—which could put pressure on an already-stretched-thin primary care system. If more clinicians leave the traditional system, it could become harder for the people who can’t pay for concierge medicine to access the traditional care they need. So while concierge medicine may help some people live healthier lives, it doesn’t yet fix the broader need for more primary care access in the United States, says Dr. Zhu.

The study also found that while concierge medicine providers are growing, the share of physicians actually declined, and the number of advanced practice providers—like nurses, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants—increased. These advanced practice providers were more likely to be new entrants to the workforce with no prior employer. So while there are still concierge providers with a career’s worth of experience, you might be more likely to get a newer provider with less experience if you opt for concierge medicine.

If you’re frustrated with a fragmented health system where you have to be the one to connect the dots between all of your doctors, concierge medicine could be a welcome reprieve. For instance, Dr. Harvey expects to see more and more patients with chronic illnesses opting for concierge models in the next couple of years. If you have a condition like PMOS, for example, you might be seeing five different specialists to deal with the symptoms: a dermatologist, endocrinologist, gynecologist, nutritionist, and a primary care provider.

With a concierge practice that specializes in convenient, wraparound care, you may be able to see multiple of these specialists all in one place, and have a health navigator or coach to help you coordinate appointments, says Dr. Bhuyan. When you’re dealing with complex medical conditions, or just finding yourself going to the doctor a lot for illnesses or infections, paying for extra time and access to your doctor might just make for a better experience.

The term “concierge” can make this form of care seem cost-prohibitive—and some services certainly are. That said, there are a few options with low membership fees that take insurance, including One Medical (starting at $9/month), Sesame Plus ($10.99/month), Tia Signature ($25-a-month membership, only available in some states) and Folx ($44/month).

If you’re using insurance, you’ll have to do your research to determine how much you’ll pay out of pocket. Popular services like Tia, Allara, Folx, and One Medical accept a wide variety of insurance plans, but specify that copays and other fees can vary plan by plan, just like at the regular doctor. If you’re not using insurance, these practices usually specify self-pay costs in addition to the membership fee depending on the visit or service type, and depending on the care you’re looking for, it could be a bargain.

Before committing to a membership anywhere, find out which services will and won’t be covered (like lab testing or imaging), and how easy it is to cancel said membership if you decide it’s not a fit, says Dr. Bhuyan.

A lot of times, you can also find local doctors practicing concierge-style medicine, and there are search tools like MDVIP or NextMD, which connect patients with a network of in-person concierge physicians all over the country. And if you can’t find one near you, there are plenty of large-scale telehealth services at your fingertips. Be sure to research the doctor beforehand to make sure that they’re legit, and that their expertise aligns with your goals, says Dr. Bhuyan.

Overall, health care is shifting more towards patients’ autonomy. They want to “decide how their health care dollars are spent, whether that's through HSA plans or other means. They’re more empowered to choose the service that works for them,” says Dr. Braunstein. So, only you can decide if a concierge doctor is right for you (and your wallet!).

Meet the experts: Jane Zhu, MD, is a primary care provider and Associate Professor of Medicine at Oregon Health and Science University. Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, is a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai. Scott Braunstein, MD, is an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care. Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the Vice President of In-Office Care at One Medical, a membership-based in-person and telehealth clinic owned by Amazon.

They’re made from a midweight fleece that feels solid enough for fall and winter, but the tapered leg and ankle cuffs give them a cleaner shape. The inside is brushed to a ridiculously soft, almost teddy-bear-like finish, so these are the pants I’d reach for when the temperature drops and I want something warm without feeling weighed down.

I wouldn’t necessarily reserve them for workouts, considering how thick they feel. But I’ve worn them for cool morning walks or days when I just want to get out of the house and move my body. The cotton-polyester blend has enough stretch to keep the tailored fit from feeling restrictive, even if you have bigger thighs. After multiple washes, they’ve held up nicely without quickly pilling. For $34, they’re also surprisingly affordable for how durable they feel. I’d just air-dry them to help keep that soft fleece feeling intact.

Nike’s dominance in activewear is undeniable, but its lineup extends to pieces that go beyond the gym. For instance, I wear this pair of sweatpants for an early-morning flight, a quick trip to pick up my dry cleaning or pretty much any day when comfort takes priority but I still want to look presentable. The inside is my favorite part, though. It’s brushed for a soft finish, making these especially good for cooler temperatures. They’re made from a cotton-polyester blend and have a standard fit that gives you room through the seat and thighs without going full baggy.

There’s no stretch woven into the fabric, but I didn’t find that to be much of an issue sitting in my cramped airplane seat. These are better suited for sport-casual days than anything involving serious movement. The open hem also gives them a cleaner, more traditional sweatpant shape rather than the tapered look of a jogger. And with sizing that goes up to 4XL, there’s a much broader range of guys who can find a comfortable fit.

Whether you’re jogging, low-impact training, or shooting hoops, Vuori’s performance pant is designed for light to moderate activities. The proprietary DreamKnit fabric is buttery soft and light, so you stay comfortable during movement. During yoga, we found that the added stretch was ideal for dynamic movements like deep lunges, twists, and stretches, where flexibility and range of motion are essential. Similar to our favorite workout shirt, its moisture-wicking properties kept us dry, preventing the pants from clinging to the body even during sweatier sessions.

True to its laid-back SoCal roots, Vuori made the fit to be relaxed and breathable, ensuring you stay cool. The tapered leg provides a modern silhouette without hugging too tightly, meaning airflow is never compromised, making these ideal for everything from exercise warm-ups to cooldowns. Beyond its performance specs, these pants simply look great on. Our editors reach for this pair to tackle last-minute errands like dry cleaning drop-offs and grocery store runs. We also appreciate the thoughtful zippered pocket on the leg—perfect for securely storing your phone or other valuables that don’t add bulk and cramp your style.

Matching Sweatshirt: Ponto Full Zip Hoodie

Relaxed fit sweatpants offer more room, better comfort. Take this pair from Reigning Champ. They offer plenty of room without looking excessively oversized. Since it's a loose fit with extra volume, I could feel the extra airflow coming up my leg, so I didn't overheat when I was lounging around like a couch potato. And the midweight terry fabric is dense but breathable, meaning it's got some heft and keeps you warm in 50-degree weather.

Unlike slim-fit sweats that hug your legs, this cut feels looser and has a straight drape that makes you look put-together and not sloppy. You don't see this often: These sweatpants have drawcord cuffs, which let you cinch them for a more tapered, jogger-like aesthetic. Wear them loose for a laid-back feel or snug for a sportier, more streamlined silhouette.

Matching Sweatshirt: Reigning Champ Midweight Terry Standard Hoodie

The whole point of sweatpants is comfort, and Uniqlo’s nailed it. For starters, the wide, straight-leg cut gives your legs and thighs ample breathing room, so you're never feeling clammy. The inside has a really smooth surface that feels cozy against the skin. The outside of the pants is equally smooth to the touch and has a polished look that makes them versatile enough for casual outings where the vibes are laid-back and not too serious. We’ve gotten plenty of use out of them for casual brunches and outdoor festivals. In addition, the elastic waistband gives you a snug, custom fit without the dreaded sag.

As the most affordable pair out of the tested options, these still measure up in quality. They’ll bring warmth in temperatures in the high 50s to low 60s, which is perfect for city commuters and everyday gym-goers. Another bonus: The front and back pockets give plenty of room to stash your essentials without worrying about them falling out.

Matching Sweatshirt: Uniqlo Sweat Oversized Pullover Hoodie

If you’re looking for something that can move from lounging to work to travel, feast your eyes on these street-ready sweatpants from Alo. Your favorite college sweats received a revamp with premium French terry on the outside and warm fleece on the interior. In fact, we found the structured fleece feels exceptionally smooth and cozy as soon as you slide the pants on, and the fit is perfect for a relaxing evening on the sofa. Also, the fabric is much thicker than others on the list, making it suitable for colder temps from winter through spring.

The straight leg keeps things polished, so you won't look like you just rolled out of bed. We styled these sweatpants with everything from a matching crewneck and hoodie for a full-on sweatsuit look. Unlike the standard relaxed cuts we’ve put through the wringer, this one is designed with an oversized fit, but doesn’t make you appear slouchy with excessive fabric.

Abercrombie makes some of the most stylish sweatpants I’ve tested, which is why I’ll be wearing them for the rest of fall. I predict that relaxed, straight-leg pants will be one of the upcoming season’s biggest trends, and this pair fits the bill. The silhouette is roomy but still looks clean enough that I don’t feel like I’m wearing straight-up pajama pants. It’s a great option for guys who don’t skip leg day.

The super-soft fleece is comfortable without being overly bulky. Instead of cinching around your ankle like a traditional jogger, the leg falls straight down and lightly drapes over your sneakers. I like the way it sits over my Asics without creating a bunch of fabric stacking around the shoe. Wear them with a T-shirt and sneakers, or go for the full matching set with Abercrombie’s coordinating hoodie. There are also plenty of colors to choose from, so you can build a set or mix them into the rest of your wardrobe.

Look for soft, breathable materials like cotton, fleece, or jersey that keep you cozy but still allow for movement. Some performance fabrics wick moisture away and provide added durability.

Your best bet will be to find options with a waistband that won’t dig in and enough room in the thighs. Different styles offer different looks and levels of comfort, and understanding the options can help you select the right pair for your needs. Here’s a breakdown of the most common sweatpant fits.

The relaxed fit is all about breathability and unlimited mobility. These sweatpants offer extra room around the hips and thighs, providing a looser feel throughout the seat. It's ideal for lounging, casual wear, and people who prioritize comfort over a tailored look. Think of it as the ultimate chill-out pant—easygoing and roomy, perfect for a lazy day, lying around the house.

Tapered sweatpants are looser at the top (around the hips and thighs) but gradually get narrower toward the ankle. This creates a more streamlined, modern silhouette for active people who want to move easily while maintaining a fashionable appearance. These pants give off a sportier vibe, perfect for gym sessions, running errands, or looking good while staying comfortable.

Slim fit sweatpants are more form-fitting and cut closer to the body, especially in the thighs and calves. They offer a sleek, minimalist look without being as tight as leggings. They’re ideal for everyday wear and even casual work settings when paired with an appropriate top.

Joggers are a type of tapered sweatpant that features a cuff at the ankle. They often have a more athletic, streetwear-inspired look and are typically made from a thinner material. The hybrid look is favored among athleisure lovers and those who like a sporty, on-the-go aesthetic. Joggers are suitable for running, light workouts, or even running errands.

Features like hidden zippered pockets enhance functionality, especially for travel. Deep side pockets can be super handy for carrying your phone, keys, wallet, earbuds, or small bills while on the go. And if you’re being a couch potato for the weekend, you can stash your remote control or snack in there as well.

Our style team, led by Style Director Christian Gollayan, put each pair through real-life scenarios: casual hangouts, city commutes, travel days, and of course, workout sessions. To keep things fair, we created a rubric and scored them across four key categories: comfort, durability, fit, and versatility.

We assessed how soft and breathable they felt, how well they survived workouts and laundry days, whether they struck the right balance between relaxed and polished, and how easily they transitioned from our homes to the streets. Bonus points went to pairs with performance perks like stretch, moisture-wicking, quick-drying, and anti-odor protection. After all was said and done, we narrowed it down to eight selections that truly stood out.

Sweatpants tend to have a looser fit throughout the leg, while joggers feature a more tailored or tapered fit. This means the legs of joggers will often touch your skin and feel a bit tight if you’ve got beefy calves.

Traditional sweatpants are often made from thicker materials like fleece and have a casual appearance, while joggers can be made from a wider range of materials, including activewear fabrics like nylon or polyester.

Joggers have ribbed cuffs at the ankles and a sportier appearance compared to the relaxed vibe of traditional sweatpants, whereas sweatpants can have either an open design or ribbed cuffs.

Sweatpants have a more relaxed and traditional look, while joggers are designed with a sporty aesthetic, often featuring modern details like zipper pockets and paneling. And because of the difference in ankle cuffs and fit, sweatpants look more casual, whereas joggers look more elevated and sleek.

Joggers are versatile for both athletic and casual wear, while sweatpants are primarily associated with casual lounging and relaxation.

Sweatpants are typically ideal for cozy indoor activities, while joggers can transition from the gym to casual outings due to their sleeker appearance.

#4891. Nvidia's Blackwell Chips Turn Up in China as Trump Floats Government Stake

Nvidia's Blackwell Chips Turn Up in China as Trump Floats Government Stake

Nvidia's most powerful chips have turned up at a Chinese data center tied to Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the scandal surrounding the company, as U.S. President Donald Trump said he could still take a government stake in the chipmaker.

Two Chinese firms installed Nvidia Blackwell hardware at the Yangtze River Delta Project, a data center in Shanghai, according to documents submitted to Chinese regulators and reviewed by Bloomberg. Blackwell chips have always required a U.S. license to ship to China.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short NVDA with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

One of the firms, Shanghai Shuoyao, offered a GB300 NVL72 rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips, as collateral for a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, Bloomberg reported. Another, Shanghai Kezhan, described a GB200 server at the site when it took out a 90 million yuan loan from a leasing firm owned by a Shanghai government agency in late 2025. Kezhan's majority owner is a Tokyo firm that Chinese outlet Caixin has said is controlled by Alice Huang.

Using the rack's serial number, Bloomberg found it was built by Taiwan's Gigabyte, which declined to say whom it originally sold the hardware to. It's unclear how the rack reached China. Shanghai Shuoyao has said it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the relationship as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation." Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company Alice Huang founded, has denied wrongdoing, and Bloomberg said it had no evidence that Megaspeed diverted hardware to the site. Nvidia did not respond to Bloomberg's questions.

Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence suspects of working with Chinese intelligence during an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, is at the center of a scandal that briefly cost him his job. The Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist this week.

Trump, who has said he "convinced" Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang, told the New York Post he was open to the U.S. government taking an equity stake in Nvidia, pointing to Intel, which handed Washington 10% of the company last year.

"I thought about it. I said, 'You know, maybe I should do it,' but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late," Trump said.

He also said a pardon for Huang was "always an option" but that he didn't think it would be necessary, and urged Huang not to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights when he appears before Congress next week. Huang is due to sit for a closed-door interview with three House committees on December 1, and to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.

Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate on Friday, Trump again said Huang was not a security threat. Asked by AFP how he could be sure when the Justice Department would not confirm it had conducted a thorough investigation, Trump said his view was based on "information I have, which is a lot of information," The Straits Times reported. "I think he's absolutely fine," he said.

Polling analyst Nate Silver said on his podcast that Trump "absolutely" could be removed from office if he profited from selling advanced chips to China, and that a roughly 25% chance of impeachment and removal priced by prediction markets was "entirely reasonable."

On Polymarket, traders put a 20% chance on Trump being impeached and removed before 2028, and a 74% chance on him being impeached before his term ends. Kalshi priced a 21% chance of Trump being impeached and removed before his term ends in January 2029.

Nvidia shares were trading at $148.74 on Friday, down 0.4% on the day, according to Yahoo! Finance. That leaves them almost 10% below Monday's close of $165.05, when the stock jumped more than 30% on Huang's return.

#4890. Nasdaq exec pushes for common EU rules on tokenized securities

Nasdaq’s Roland Chai backed exploring common EU rules for tokenized securities and said its Swedish subsidiary had applied for a DLT license.

Roland Chai, executive vice president and head of digital liquidity networks at Nasdaq, urged European Union lawmakers to explore creating a dedicated legal framework for tokenized securities to avoid legal uncertainties arising from fragmented regulations.

“We do see merit in exploring a 28th regime for dedicated, harmonized EU-level framework for tokenized securities issuance,” Chai said, speaking at the European Commission’s tokenization roundtable in Brussels on Thursday.

The term “28th regime” refers to the concept of an optional EU-wide set of rules that would apply alongside the national systems of the bloc’s 27 member states.

Chai said that Nasdaq’s Swedish subsidiary had applied for its first distributed ledger technology (DLT) trading and settlement license. Nasdaq was also considering accepting tokenized collateral, but faced constraints under current EU rules.

Chai’s comments echo a recent warning from European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who said Friday that Europe risks developing a fragmented tokenized securities market unless it establishes common standards. Without them, trading platforms could be unable to settle transactions with one another.

Related: Swiss central bank, UBS and SIX study ledger for tokenized settlement

BlackRock’s head of digital cash Hannah Winter said institutional clients seeking access to regulated money market funds were driving demand for tokenization.

“For us it’s absolutely demand-driven,” Winter said at the roundtable. “The ability to leverage a tokenized money market fund increases the return on those balances, but also frees up the ability for operations to be unlocked on a 24/7 basis.”

Winter said the primary uses of tokenized funds include treasury and liquidity management, as well as collateral for derivatives positions.

In August, BlackRock announced plans to offer tokenized versions of select European money market funds using JPMorgan’s blockchain infrastructure, including pound sterling, euro and US dollar share classes from BlackRock’s Institutional Cash Series.

BlackRock’s BUIDL fund, total assets under management and monthly returns. Source: RWA.xyz

BlackRock launched its first tokenized US dollar-denominated institutional liquidity fund, BUIDL, in March 2024. The fund had $1.55 billion in assets, down nearly 30% over the past 30 days, and a trailing one-year return of 3.59%, according to RWA.xyz.
